claims.text: A machine-learning interatomic potential trained on extensive ab initio liquid snapshots can replace traditional EAM references in thermodynamic integration.
Replacing EAM references with the trained MLIP will markedly reduce phase-space mismatch in high-temperature multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The proposed MLIP is a deep neural-network potential trained on ab initio configurations from both solid and liquid states, with emphasis on diverse high-temperature liquid configurations.
The method is applicable to equiatomic or nearly equiatomic alloys containing at least four principal elements.
The proposed temperature range is 0.95–1.0 times the melting temperature.
The MLIP will provide smoother and more complete energy-landscape sampling than EAM.
Training on many ab initio liquid configurations will make the MLIP more faithful to the high-dimensional energy landscape of a multicomponent liquid.
A more faithful MLIP energy landscape will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
Improved phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to less adaptable EAM references.
Continuous differentiability and physical realism of the MLIP contribute to reducing thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The MLIP reference could reduce thermodynamic-integration path errors by approximately a factor of ten relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
TOR-TILD EAM references exhibit substantial thermodynamic-integration path mismatch because they represent liquid configurational diversity inadequately.
The approach is expected to work best for high-entropy alloys whose constituent elements have similar atomic sizes and bonding characteristics.
Performance may deteriorate far above melting or when relevant configurations are under-represented in the training data.
The magnitude of mismatch reduction depends on the density and quality of the ab initio training configurations.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing MLIP-assisted thermodynamic integration with direct ab initio thermodynamic integration and an EAM-based baseline near the melting temperature.

Failure to obtain an approximately order-of-magnitude reduction in path mismatch relative to EAM, or observation of systematic deviations from direct ab initio results beyond acceptable error margins, would falsify the hypothesis.
